rows.answer: Yesterday I saw that film.
rows.feedback: Your sentence is correct, but the word order can be improved by placing 'yesterday' at the end of the sentence.

rows.answer: I seen that film yesterday.
rows.feedback: Use 'saw' instead of 'seen' because the sentence is about something that happened in the past.

rows.answer: I did see that film yesterday.
rows.feedback: Your sentence is correct, but using 'I saw' is more natural here.

rows.answer: He had finished his homework two hours ago.
rows.feedback: Use the past simple tense for actions completed in the past. Try: 'He finished his homework two hours ago.'

rows.answer: I am learning English for five years.
rows.feedback: Use the present perfect continuous tense to show an action that started in the past and continues now. Try: 'I have been learning English for five years.'

rows.answer: I have been studying English for five years.
rows.feedback: Use 'learning' instead of 'studying' to match the original sentence's meaning.

rows.answer: My sister is engineer.
rows.feedback: You forgot to use the correct article 'an' before 'engineer' because it starts with a vowel sound.

rows.answer: Mount Everest is highest mountain in the world.
rows.feedback: Add 'the' before 'highest mountain' to make it correct.

rows.answer: Everest is the highest mountain in the world.
rows.feedback: You're correct to remove the article. The name of a specific mountain doesn't need 'the'.

rows.answer: I'll meet you at bus stop.
rows.feedback: Add 'the' before 'bus stop' to make it sound natural.

rows.answer: We arrived at London late at night.
rows.feedback: Use 'in' when arriving in a city or country. Try again!

rows.answer: We got to London late at night.
rows.feedback: Use 'in' instead of 'to' when arriving in a city or country. Your sentence is natural and correct otherwise.

rows.answer: My brother is more taller than me.
rows.feedback: Use 'taller' instead of 'more taller' for comparing height. Try again!

rows.answer: This book is more interesting then the film.
rows.feedback: Use 'than' when comparing two things. Try again!

rows.answer: Your car is more faster than my car.
rows.feedback: Use 'faster' instead of 'more faster' for correct comparative form.

rows.answer: They are not playing football every Saturday.
rows.feedback: Use 'don't' instead of 'are not' for the negative form in present simple tense.

rows.answer: When I see him, I will tell him.
rows.feedback: Use 'If' instead of 'When' for real possibilities. Try again!

rows.answer: If she studied harder, she will pass the exam.
rows.feedback: In second conditionals, the main clause uses 'would' for hypothetical results. Try: 'If she studied harder, she would pass the exam.'

rows.answer: If I knew her number, I can call her.
rows.feedback: Use 'could' in the main clause for an unreal situation. Try again.

rows.answer: I knows the answer.
rows.feedback: Use 'know' instead of 'knows' because 'I' needs the base form of the verb.
